item.title: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ … There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … There are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.98
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Lakuṇṭaka-Bhaddiya: “Outside the parks, At the Ambāṭaka woodland, In the forest with its groves, Having abandoned craving, the root of craving, Bhaddiya sits in…
item.description:
Elder Lakuṇṭaka-Bhaddiya:

“Outside the parks,
At the Ambāṭaka woodland,
In the forest with its groves,
Having abandoned craving, the root of craving,
Bhaddiya sits in meditation —
Blissful, happy.”

Some people delight
In drums, flutes, and cymbals.
But I, at the root of a tree,
Delight in the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Buddha grants a gift,
I receive that gift.
I bear mindfulness of the body,
Constantly in all realms.

Those who mock me for my body,
Or follow me for my voice —
They do not know me,
Driven by sensual desire.

Not knowing the inside,
Not seeing the outside —
Blocked on all sides, the fool
Is carried away by words.

Not knowing the inside,
But seeing the outside —
Seeing only the external fruit,
He too is carried away by words.

Knowing the inside with wisdom,
Seeing the outside as well —
Seeing without obstruction,
He is not carried away by words.

From: Theragāthā 7.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great harm as heedlessness. Heedlessness, monks, leads to great harm.”
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great harm as heedlessness. Heedlessness, monks, leads to great harm.”

item.title: “Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached…
item.description:
“Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached to form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. And, monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, and the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, they have not, monks, escaped from this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans; they are not free from it, not detached, not liberated, their minds are not at ease. But when they directly know these five aggregates … as they actually are, then they have escaped … their minds are at ease.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.28
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them,…
item.description:
“Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, then delight ceases. With the cessation of delight, lust ceases. With the cessation of lust, bondage ceases. Not being bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells alone.’ Even if he lives in the midst of a village crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, ascetics of other sects and their disciples — still he is called ‘one who dwells alone.’ Why? Because craving, the companion, has been abandoned by him. Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells alone.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.63
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual…
item.description:
“Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual desire is abandoned; when the mind of ill-will exists, that ill-will is abandoned; when the mind of anger exists, that anger is abandoned; when the mind of hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity … heedlessness exists, that heedlessness is abandoned … Monks, I say that if he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic, he can abandon the defilements that are stains of an ascetic, blemishes of an ascetic, faults of an ascetic, leading to a plane of misery, to a bad destination, to the taking up of an evil realm. He sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated. Because he sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated, gladness arises; from gladness, joy; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; from bodily tranquility, he experiences ease; from ease, the mind becomes concentrated. I say that it is because of inner mental concentration that he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 40 – Cūḷa-Assapurasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, for one whose greed is not abandoned, whose hatred is not abandoned, whose delusion is not abandoned — he is called one who is…
item.description:
“Monks, for one whose greed is not abandoned, whose hatred is not abandoned, whose delusion is not abandoned — he is called one who is bound by Māra, trapped in Māra’s snare, subject to the Evil One’s will.

But, monks, for one whose greed is abandoned, whose hatred is abandoned, whose delusion is abandoned — he is called one not bound by Māra, freed from Māra’s snare, not subject to the Evil One’s will.

One who has abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion,
Him they call one with a developed mind,
One who has become Brahmā, the Tathāgata, the Buddha,
The one who has overcome enmity and fear,
The one who has abandoned all — such a one is called thus.”

From: Itivuttaka 68
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: - Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound.…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
- Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound. Some are bound with ropes, some with chains, some with shackles.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the meaning of this, on that occasion recited this verse:
The wise say that such binding
Is not strong —
Binding with iron, with ropes,
With wooden shackles —
But infatuation with sensual pleasures,
With jewels and ornaments,
And anxious thoughts
Directed toward children and wives —
The wise say this binding
Is truly strong.
Though it drags one down,
Subtle and hard to escape,
True renunciants cut it in two,
Without wishing or longing,
Abandoning all sensual pleasures.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.10
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “What is wandering without a standing place? The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of forms, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata,…
item.description:
“What is wandering without a standing place? The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of forms, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, so that it cannot arise again in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a standing place.’ The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of sounds … smells … tastes … touches … phenomena, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata … Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a standing place.’ Thus, householder, is wandering without a standing place.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Speak with a person Who holds a sword in hand, Speak with a demon, Or sit closely with them. A poisonous snake — If bitten,…
item.description:
Speak with a person
Who holds a sword in hand,
Speak with a demon,
Or sit closely with them.
A poisonous snake —
If bitten, one dies —
But do not alone
Speak with a woman.
Mindless, they bind one
With glances, with smiles,
With revealing clothes,
With sweet words —
Still not satisfied,
One becomes unconscious and dies.
These five strands of sensual pleasure
Are seen in female form —
Form, sound, smell, taste, touch —
Enticing and agreeable.
Overwhelmed by the waterfall of sensuality,
Flooded and swept away,
The foolish and ignorant,
Not understanding sensual pleasures.
Humans, at death,
Go to states of existence and non-existence —
They are led on
Through many births.
Those who understand sensual pleasures,
Without fear in their conduct,
Reach the far shore,
Attaining the destruction of the defilements.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.55
📖 Read this sutta
